title: OOM cascade and memory throttling runbook
author: Priya Nair
content:
Summary:
This runbook defines the operational play for diagnosing and recovering from OOM (Out Of Memory) cascades and memory-pressure-induced throttling in the serving runtime. It covers detection signals, immediate mitigation (fast-path recovery), medium-term capacity and configuration changes, and post-incident SLO/error-budget reconciliation. This is intended for SREs on-call for model-serving and runtime engineers supporting quantized and multi-tenant GPUs.

When to use this runbook:
- Multiple worker processes failing with OOM within a short window (minutes).
- Sustained memory pressure across a node pool leading to eviction or throttling signals (OOM_kill, slow-model spins).
- Unexplained latency spikes correlated with memory metrics or KV cache growth.
- Alerts: memory.node.high (>= 90% for 3m), worker.oom.rate (>5% of workers in 2m), kvcache.evictions.rate (>10% in 5m).

Key metrics and thresholds (single-pane reference):
- node.memory.utilization (gauge): warn at 75%, critical at 90% measured across 1m aggregates.
- worker.oom.count (counter): alert if >= 3 within 5 minutes in same cluster zone.
- kvcache.size.bytes (gauge): action if growth rate > 10%/minute sustained for 5 minutes.
- request.tail_latency_99_ms (histogram): correlate when increases > 2x baseline for 5+ minutes.
- slo.error_budget_burn_rate (gauge): if burn_rate > 2x and memory alerts active, escalate to tier-2.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes) — Tier 0 (on-call responder):
1) Confirm alerts and scope:
   - Query service map: which services/tenants are affected?
   - Grafana/Observe: check node.memory.utilization and OOM events.
   - Run: kubectl get pods -n model-serving -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running | grep <suspect-node>
2) Identify immediate impact on SLOs:
   - Check per-route error and latency dashboards (last 15m).
   - Pull error budget burn rate for affected SLOs.
3) If OOM events are ongoing, execute mitigation steps below immediately.

Immediate mitigation steps (fast-path) — Tier 1 (SRE with runtime privileges):
A) Soft remediation (non-disruptive, prefer first):
   - Remove heavy queries from the live traffic gate: update /traffic-gates route rules to reject or sample-down very large requests (> max_tokens threshold).
   - Enable per-request memory limits where supported: set request.max_kv_bytes=128MB for affected model routes.
   - Apply priority class to critical routes to preserve control-plane operations.
B) Node-level containment (if soft remediation insufficient):
   - cordon the affected node(s): kubectl cordon <node>
   - migrate non-critical pods off the node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
   - scale up transient capacity (if autoscaler policy allows burst): trigger autoscaler burst: POST /internal/autoscaler/v1/burst?policy=oom-emergency&count=2
C) Worker restart pattern (when a single process is leaking or stuck):
   - Rolling restart of model-worker on the node: kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-worker --namespace=model-serving --field-selector=spec.nodeName=<node>
   - Use restart guard to ensure not to thrash: wait 60s between restarts and monitor worker.oom.count.

Medium-term recovery and remediation — Tier 2 (SRE + Runtime Eng):
1) Capture forensic evidence before any destructive action:
   - Collect coredumps (if enabled), dmesg logs, /var/log/messages, and container logs for the time window (t0-10m to t0+10m).
   - Snapshot process memory maps: pmap/pidstat or jmap for JVM-based model processes.
   - Save KV cache metrics and a sample of cache keys (respecting PII constraints).
2) Analyze root cause hypotheses (quick checklist):
   - Genuine workload spike (larger prompts / more concurrent long-context requests).
   - KV cache runaway due to misconfigured prefix retention or tenant key duplication.
   - Memory leak in new model binary or a third-party dependency (libsomething).
   - Node-level hardware degradation (failing NUMA behavior or GPU driver memory accounting bug).
3) Remediation options by cause:
   - Workload spike: enforce request size guardrails, add token-based admission control, and advise product/CS to throttle heavy tenants.
   - KV cache runaway: reduce retention window, enable max_entries limit and promote explicit cache eviction policy. Example config change (YAML):
     kvCache:
       enabled: true
       maxEntries: 250000
       evictionPolicy: LRU
       retentionSeconds: 1800
   - Memory leak in binary: pin to previous version and schedule canary deploys with heap/proc-accounting instrumentation.
   - Hardware/driver: isolate to node pool, tag and retire suspect hosts; file vendor ticket with kernel/OEM vendor.

Capacity planning triggers and actions:
- If we observe node.memory.utilization > 75% baseline frequently (>= 3 days of >40% of daily peaks above 75%), schedule capacity runway provisioning for the service and increase reserve by 15% for that service's cluster pool.
- For models with >100 active concurrent long-context requests, request dedicated GPU pools via Dedicated capacity quota.
- Maintain a 10% memory headroom buffer on all serving node pools running quantized models due to heavier KV-backed footprints.

Operational tooling and commands (copy-paste safe snippets):
- Identify recent OOM events:
  kubectl logs -n model-serving --since=15m -l app=model-worker | grep -E "OOM|OutOfMemory|KilledProcess"
- Correlate with node memory metrics (Prometheus):
  sum by(instance) (rate(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes[2m]))
- Force-cache-eviction RPC (internal service):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://internal-api.redwood/v1/cache/evict?scope=tenant:<tenant-id>&policy=soft
- Burst autoscaler API (internal):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"policy":"oom-emergency","count":3}' https://internal-api.redwood/internal/autoscaler/v1/burst

Incident review and SLO/error-budget reconciliation:
1) Assign the incident a severity label and owner within 48 hours.
2) Collect timeline and evidence: alerts, key metrics, tool commands executed, and configuration changes.
3) Calculate SLO impact: compute time-windowed error budget consumption and attach to incident record.
4) If error budget burn > 25% for the impacted SLO, require a corrective action plan and capacity provisioning proposal within 7 days.
5) Include the following in the post-incident report:
   - Exact root cause (or top hypotheses) and evidence for each.
   - List of mitigation steps taken and the time to restore.
   - Long-term fixes, owner, and ETA.
   - SLO impact summary (tokens affected, estimated customer impact, error budget consumed).

Runbook for recurring / chronic memory events (continuous-improvement loop):
1) If the same cause reappears more than twice in 30 days, open a reliability initiative ticket (RI) and prioritize a fix in the next SRE cycle.
2) RI deliverables should include: automated canary with memory leak detection, KV cache instrumentation, and a traffic-shepherd rule to limit large requests.
3) Add synthetic canaries that exercise long-context flows at low volume but regular cadence to detect growth in memory footprint.

Incident checklist (to attach to incident ticket):
- [ ] Node(s) cordoned and drained where appropriate
- [ ] Forensic logs archived to incident bucket (s3://redwood-incidents/<id>/logs)
- [ ] Core dumps collected and uploaded (if policy allows)
- [ ] KV cache snapshot collected
- [ ] Autoscaler actions documented
- [ ] SLO impact computed and attached
- [ ] Owners assigned for short and long term fixes

Appendix: example alert rule (Prometheus-style pseudo):
- alert: NodeMemoryPressureHigh
  expr: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes) / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes > 0.9
  for: 3m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Node memory > 90% for >3m"

Appendix: KV cache config table (human-readable):
| parameter | default | recommended for quantized-serving | rationale |
| maxEntries | 100000 | 250000 | Quantized models maintain larger key footprints; raise default carefully |
| retentionSeconds | 3600 | 1800 | Shorter retention reduces runaway growth during spikes |
| evictionPolicy | LRU | LRU | Proven policy for tenant fairness |
| trackPerTenant | false | true | Helps prevent a single tenant from polluting global cache |

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary on-call: model-serving SRE rotation (pager) — first responder.
- Secondary: runtime-engineering (pager).
- Triage lead: SRE duty lead or on-call manager for multi-tenant incidents.
- Escalate to incident commander for Sev2+ when burn rate > 2x or when > 5% of customers report functional degradation.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: Priya Nair (runtime SRE lead).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev1/Sev2 OOM incident.
- Change log: last major update 2026-06-15 — added KV cache retention guidance and autoscaler burst policy.

- KV cache design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/kv-cache-design-2025

End of runbook.
